events.title: Protectorate treaties on the Ivorian coast
hints: Naval officers signed protectorate treaties with local kings at two coastal trading posts.
France built forts at Grand-Bassam and Assinie to secure trade.
The treaties gave France a first foothold on a coast named for the commodity traders came to buy.
events.summary: In 1843-1844 Admiral Bouët-Willaumez signed treaties with the rulers of Grand-Bassam and Assinie that placed the coast under French protection and allowed forts and trading posts, the first step towards a colony.

events.title: French Ivory Coast colony
hints: Settler-owned and African-owned plantations drove a cash-crop economy in this French colony.
Cocoa, coffee and tropical timber were its main exports.
A colony formally created in 1893, it became independent in 1960 under a leader who had campaigned against forced labour.
events.summary: France made the territory a colony in 1893. Cocoa, coffee and timber became the main exports, grown on plantations that relied heavily on conscripted and migrant labour. Independence came in 1960.

events.title: Forced labour on colonial plantations
hints: Under a colonial legal code, villagers could be conscripted for roads, railways and European plantations.
Workers were brought south from a poorer inland colony to staff plantations.
A 1946 law pushed through by a local planter-politician abolished forced labour across French Africa.
events.summary: Under the indigénat, Africans in the colony were conscripted for public works and for work on European-owned plantations and logging camps, with many workers moved south from Upper Volta. Forced labour ended after a 1946 law championed by Félix Houphouët-Boigny.
